verdict.reasoning: Patient reports being wheezy and short of breath for 2–3 days: "recently I'm wheezy. Uh, I have feel like kind of short of breath" and when asked duration: "Mmm, two, three days. Yeah, quite recently."
Patient states: "I have, I have cough and cough a lot".
Patient says: "I have a fever" and later clarifies temperature: "Yes, I checked, I have fever" then "What was your temperature?" "Uh, thirty seven, yeah."

Dyspnea on exertion and inability to walk to work are described: "I also used to walk to work but recently I can't because... I feel like very short of breath" and doctor asks about sitting vs walking, patient: "Just walk or sometimes, but currently I feel, I feel well."

Patient notes difficulty finishing sentences: "sometimes I feel like I can't even finish sentence is quite difficult to, to complete the, the the talking sometimes" and later confirms: "Doctor: did you say you were finding it hard to complete your sentences? Patient: Yeah, sometimes."
When asked about night symptoms: "Doctor: Have you been woken up at night time at all? Patient: No, just daytime working, yeah."

Patient denies chest pain, sputum, and blood: "Doctor: Have you coughed any phlegm up or anything like that? Patient: No." "Any, any, um, blood in there when you cough? Patient: No, I don't think so." "Doctor: Any chest pain? Patient: No chest pain, no."

History of significant childhood asthma with hospital visits: "Patient: Uh, yes, I had asthma..." "Doctor: when you were a child how bad was your asthma? Patient: Uh, it's quite bad." "Doctor: did you ever have to go to hospital with it? Patient: Yeah, sometimes." and no ICU: "No, not that bad but still, sometimes, need to go to hospital."
Patient twice reports hay fever: "I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema" and later: "Doctor: Any other medical problems? Patient: Uh, I have, uh, hay fever as well."
Patient mentions eczema: "I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema, sorry."

Use of salbutamol as needed every few weeks and with exercise: "Patient: Um, I took salbutamol? Salbutamol? Yeah." "Doctor: you normally take that do you? Or is that just recently? Patient: Normally, yeah." "Doctor: how often do you normally need it? Patient: Every, every few weeks?" and "Doctor: What about when you exercise normally, do you have to use medication? Uh, inhalers? Patient: Yeah, yeah, a bit."
No other medications: "Doctor: um, and do you take any other medications? Patient: No, nothing else."
No drug allergies: "Doctor: And any allergies to medications? Patient: No, no allergies."
Non-smoker: "Doctor: Do you smoke? Patient: No, I don't smoke."

Alcohol intake described as 1 glass every 2–3 days: "Doctor: Do you drink any alcohol regularly? Patient: Yeah, one glass." then "Doctor: Every, how often did you say? Patient: Every two or three days? Depends, yeah." and "one glass of wine."

Living situation and job are given; working from home is described: "Patient: I live with my partner." and "Patient: Uh, I'm engineer." plus "recently I, I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave, yeah." which supports that they work as an engineer and currently work from home.

Doctor assesses asthma flare with 2–3 days of wheeze/SOB, history of asthma, and SABA use: "Doctor: it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma"; symptoms earlier:  "recently I'm wheezy... short of breath" "two, three days"; and salbutamol use: "I took salbutamol... Normally, yeah... Every, every few weeks..."

Allergic rhinitis/hay fever considered as trigger: "Doctor: it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma. It could be, um, triggered by, if there's more pollen around" and patient has hay fever: "I also had, uh, hay fever"; later plan includes antihistamine for this.

Eczema is part of atopic history considered in assessment: patient: "I also had, uh, hay fever and eczema"; the doctor later discusses asthma/hay fever/antihistamine together, indicating atopic background is relevant to assessment.
Dose escalation of SABA: "Doctor: if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like, every four hours? Initially".

Spacer to be prescribed and taught: "Doctor: Have you got, um, a spacer at home?" Patient: "No." "Doctor: OK. Um, what I can do is, I can prescribe you... a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up."

Peak flow meter prescription and 1-week monitoring: "Doctor: I can prescribe you a peak flow meter so we can check your breathing level" and later: "when you get the peak flow meter... if you can record a value first thing when you wake up... And in the evening over the next week, and then we can discuss that over the phone".

Safety-net advice: "Doctor: if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway so we can just advise you further with that." Worsening SOB is implied as part of wheezing/flare; high fever explicitly mentioned.

Review in about a week and consider controller inhaler: "Doctor: it will be a good idea when you're feeling better if we can arrange just a review... because we may need to start some other medication for you." and "You could arrange a review in a week or so" and later linked to peak flow review: "then we can discuss that over the phone... and see whether you need to go on another inhaler as well."
Start regular OTC antihistamine: "Doctor: OK, and the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine. Which you can get from the pharmacy, I can put a on your notes about what to take."

Follow-up in ~1 week or sooner if worse: "You could arrange a review in a week or so" and earlier: "if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway" indicating earlier review if symptoms worsen.
